primary_diagnosis: Iron-deficiency anemia from occult gastrointestinal blood loss
clinical_reasoning_summary: The patient’s chronic anemia, markedly elevated platelet distribution width, and metabolic risk profile point most strongly toward iron‑deficiency anemia secondary to occult gastrointestinal blood loss. Metabolic syndrome contributes to a moderate risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and early chronic kidney disease. Untreated anxiety is well documented. Other possibilities (OSA, NAFLD, MPN, subclinical hypothyroidism, occult upper GI malignancy) are less likely based on current evidence but remain on the differential pending targeted testing.
unresolved_findings: Elevated platelet distribution width (PDW) 245.9 fL – magnitude atypical for simple reactive thrombocytosis
Mild hyperkalaemia (5.1 mmol/L) with rising trend – partially explained by lisinopril but renal contribution uncertain
recommended_workup: Complete iron studies (serum ferritin, iron, total iron‑binding capacity, transferrin saturation)
Fecal occult blood test and, if positive, colonoscopy
Upper endoscopy (EGD) to evaluate for upper GI sources of bleeding
Lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
Serum creatinine with eGFR calculation and urine albumin‑to‑creatinine ratio
Overnight polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing
Hepatic ultrasound or FibroScan to assess for fatty liver disease
Repeat CBC with platelet indices to monitor PDW and platelet count trends
If PDW remains markedly elevated after iron repletion, consider JAK2 V617F mutation testing for myeloproliferative neoplasm
